summary: Specifies how to set up and maintain pseudowires, which emulate Layer 2 services such as Frame Relay, ATM and Ethernet over an MPLS network, using extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). Encapsulation details are in companion documents. It is a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 8077.

eli5.summary: A pseudowire is like a pretend cable running through a bigger network. This note says how the routers agree to set one up. A newer note replaced it.

questions: how to signal pseudowires over mpls
how does ldp set up a pseudowire
what is the pwid fec element
subtitle: How routers use LDP to set up and maintain pseudowires that carry Layer 2 traffic across an MPLS network.

tldr.problem: Layer 2 services such as Frame Relay, ATM and Ethernet can be carried over an MPLS backbone inside pseudowires, but the two edge routers need a way to agree on which label identifies which pseudowire.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4447 extends the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) with two new FEC element types (0x80 and 0x81), a PW Status TLV and new status codes, so each endpoint can bind an MPLS label to a pseudowire and tell the other endpoint about it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4447 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8077, so new work should follow that document.

today: RFC 4447 has been obsoleted by RFC 8077, which is the document to follow now. It was also updated by RFC 6723, RFC 6870 and RFC 7358.

sections.title: Pseudowires over an MPLS Network
sections.content:
A pseudowire emulates a Layer 2 service, such as Frame Relay, ATM or Ethernet, across an MPLS-enabled network. It can also carry low-rate Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) and SONET circuit emulation. The Layer 2 frames are encapsulated, given a pseudowire header, and sent through a tunnel across the network. How frames are encapsulated is left to companion documents.

RFC 4447 covers only the control side: how the two edge routers (PEs) set up and maintain the pseudowire using extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). It defines no new LDP messages. It adds new TLVs, FEC elements, parameters and status codes. It deals only with point-to-point pseudowires and does not discuss quality of service.

In the reference model, a customer device connects to a PE over an attachment circuit (AC). The PE sends traffic over a pseudowire to the remote PE, which delivers it out of its own attachment circuit. The RFC treats PE1 as the ingress router and PE2 as the egress router for a given frame.
sections.eli5: Two houses want a private tube between them, even though the tube runs through a busy city. This note says how the two houses talk to each other to set that tube up.

sections.title: The Pseudowire Label
sections.content:
The core idea is that the demultiplexor field of the pseudowire is an MPLS label, called the PW label. The sending PE puts the PW label on the frame. If the tunnel is an MPLS LSP, it pushes a tunnel label on top. The PW label stays at the bottom of the label stack and is not seen again until the packet reaches the far PE, which uses it to decide which pseudowire, and therefore which attachment circuit, the frame belongs to. For an ATM AAL5 frame that might mean an outgoing interface and a VPI/VCI value. For Frame Relay it means an interface and a DLCI.

A large number of pseudowires can share one tunnel, so the network core never keeps state for individual pseudowires. Labels MUST come from the per-platform label space. It is REQUIRED that the same PW ID and PW type are assigned for a circuit in both directions, while the group ID need not match.

LDP assigns and distributes the PW label. An LDP session must run between the two endpoints, found with the Extended Discovery mechanism. LDP MUST be used in downstream unsolicited mode, and liberal label retention SHOULD be used. Static assignment of PW labels is also allowed, and implementations SHOULD support it. Each FEC TLV MUST contain exactly one FEC element, and the Generic Label TLV MUST be used.
sections.eli5: Each tube gets a number sticker. The router at the far end reads the sticker to know which tube a package came through and where to hand it over.

sections.title: The PWid and Generalized PWid FEC Elements
sections.content:
Two FEC element types identify a pseudowire inside an LDP Label Mapping message. Only one is used for any given pseudowire.

The PWid FEC element (type 0x80) is used when both endpoints have been provisioned with the same 32-bit identifier. It carries a control word bit (C), a 15-bit PW type, a PW information length, a 32-bit Group ID, a non-zero 32-bit PW ID and optional interface parameter sub-TLVs. Each endpoint starts a unidirectional LSP, and an outgoing and incoming LSP are bound into one pseudowire when they share the same PW ID and PW type.

The Generalized PWid FEC element (type 0x81) identifies each endpoint with structured, variable-length attachment identifiers: an Attachment Group Identifier (AGI), a Source AII (SAII) and a Target AII (TAII). The AGI is the same at both ends, while the AII differs. A bidirectional pseudowire is two LSPs whose FECs have the SAII and TAII swapped. Its grouping function and interface parameters move into the optional PW Grouping ID TLV (0x096C) and Interface Parameters TLV (0x096B).

Interface parameters carry facts such as the attachment circuit MTU. The Interface MTU sub-TLV is a 2-octet value and is REQUIRED for packet-carrying PW types. If it does not match in both directions, the pseudowire MUST NOT be enabled. An optional interface description string can be 0 to 80 octets of UTF-8 text. Because the sub-TLV is part of the FEC, it cannot change during the life of the pseudowire.
sections.eli5: Each tube has a name tag. The simple tag is one shared number. The fancier tag spells out who is at each end, so the routers can work out which tube is meant.

sections.title: Signaling Pseudowire Status
sections.content:
PEs MUST send Label Mapping messages as soon as a pseudowire is configured and administratively enabled, whatever the state of the attachment circuit. The label should not be withdrawn unless an operator configures the pseudowire down or deletes it. Status changes are then reported with the PW Status TLV (0x096A), which holds a 4-octet status code. Each bit of the status code can be set independently so several faults can be reported at once, and a fault is cleared by sending a notification with that bit cleared. The lowest bit, PW Not Forwarding, is a generic failure indication for link-down events that no other bit covers.

The TLV travels in an LDP Notification message whose Status TLV code is 0x00000028 (PW status). A PE can send one wild card status message for many pseudowires by giving only a group ID, or only the PW Grouping ID TLV, and setting the PW information length to 0. This is OPTIONAL to send, but all PEs implementing it are REQUIRED to accept it.

When a pseudowire is first set up the PEs MUST try to negotiate use of the PW Status TLV. A PE that supports it MUST include it in its initial Label Mapping. If the remote PE does not include one, both fall back to the older label withdraw method, where the Label Mapping is advertised only while the attachment circuit is active.
sections.eli5: The two routers keep each other posted about whether the tube is working, like two friends with tin cans who say 'I can hear you' or 'the string is broken'.

sections.title: Control Word Negotiation and Label Reuse
sections.content:
The C bit in the FEC says whether the pseudowire uses a control word. For PW types where the control word is REQUIRED, Label Mapping messages MUST have c=1, and a received mapping with c=0 triggers a Label Release with the status code Illegal C-bit, so the pseudowire is not enabled.

For other PW types, each endpoint MUST be configurable as PREFERRED or NOT PREFERRED for the control word, and the RFC does not say which default to use. If a mapping with c=0 has been received, the PE replies with c=0. If it received c=1 and prefers the control word, it replies with c=1. Otherwise it sends its own preference and waits. A c=0 mapping that arrives after sending c=1 is answered with a Label Withdraw carrying the Wrong C-bit status code, followed by a Label Mapping with c=0. The outcome is that the control word is used only if both ends prefer it.

When sequence numbers are in use, a released label must not be re-advertised until old packets are unlikely still to be in the network. Otherwise the egress router could see a stale packet with a sequence number between 1 and 32768 and wrongly reject packets. Suggested fixes are to advertise a different PW label or to wait long enough before re-advertising.
sections.eli5: Before using a special header, both routers must agree. If one says no, they both skip it, just like a game that only uses an extra rule when everyone wants it.

sections.title: Data-Plane and Control-Plane Security
sections.content:
The RFC treats the data plane and the control plane separately. For the data plane, a pseudowire over MPLS should be at least as secure as the Layer 2 network it emulates. The MPLS network SHOULD be isolated so that outsiders cannot insert MPLS packets, and it should not accept MPLS packets from external interfaces unless the top label was legitimately distributed to the sender. The three main problems are spoofing, alteration and inspection, because the encapsulation by itself provides no authentication, integrity or privacy.

For the control plane, the considerations in RFC 3036 apply. An incoming LDP session request MUST NOT be accepted unless its source address belongs to an eligible LDP peer, and some means of preventing source address spoofing must be in place. The LDP MD5 authentication option MUST be implemented and should be used for stronger security. It gives integrity and authentication but not privacy, and because it uses pre-shared keys it gives little protection against replay and can be hard to deploy with auto-configuration.
sections.eli5: Only let routers you know build tubes with you, and check their name tag, or a stranger could plug your tube into the wrong place.

fields.name: PWid (0x80)
fields.desc: FEC element type for the PWid FEC.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: 1 means a control word is present on this pseudowire.

fields.name: PW info Length
fields.desc: Length of the PW ID and interface parameters in octets; 0 means all pseudowires in the group.

fields.name: Group ID
fields.desc: Arbitrary value that groups pseudowires, for example by port.

fields.name: PW ID
fields.desc: Non-zero connection ID that, with the PW type, identifies the pseudowire.
